danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Ruslands kejser havde imens opholdt sig i Vilna i mere end en måned, hvor han inspicerede tropper og afholdt manøvrer. Intet var klar til den krig, alle ventede, og som kejseren var rejst fra Petersborg for at forberede. Der var ingen overordnet krigsplan. Vaklen mellem de forskellige planer, der var foreslået, var endda taget til, efter at kejseren havde været ved hovedkvarteret i en måned. Hver af de tre hære havde sin egen øverstkommanderende, men der var ingen øverstbefalende over alle styrkerne, og kejseren påtog sig ikke selv dette ansvar.

Jo længere kejseren forblev i Vilna, desto mindre forberedte alle sig — trætte af at vente — på krigen. Alle anstrengelser fra dem, der omgav kejseren, syntes kun rettet mod at få ham til at tilbringe tiden behageligt og glemme, at krig var forestående.

I juni, efter mange baller og fester givet af de polske magnater, hoffet og kejseren selv, faldt det en af de polske adjudanter i kejserens følge ind, at adjudanterne burde give en middag og et bal for kejseren. Ideen blev ivrigt modtaget. Kejseren gav sit samtykke. Adjudanterne samlede penge ind ved tegning. Den dame, der ansås for mest behagelig for kejseren, blev inviteret til at fungere som værtinde. Grev Bennigsen, der var godsejer i Vilna-provinsen, tilbød sit landsted til festen, og den trettende juni blev fastsat til bal, middag, regatta og fyrværkeri på Zakret, grev Bennigsens landsæde.

Netop den dag Napoleon udstedte ordren om at krydse Njemen, og hans fortrop, der drev kosakkerne for sig, krydsede den russiske grænse, tilbragte Alexander aftenen ved den fest, hans adjudanter gav på Bennigsens landsæde.

Det var en munter og strålende fest. Kendere af sådanne sager erklærede, at sjældent havde så mange smukke kvinder været samlet ét sted. Grevinde Bezukhova (Hélène) var til stede blandt andre russiske damer, der havde fulgt kejseren fra Petersborg til Vilna, og fordunklede de raffinerede polske damer med sin massive, såkaldt russiske type af skønhed. Kejseren bemærkede hende og beærede hende med en dans.

Boris Drubetskoj, der havde efterladt sin hustru i Moskva og for øjeblikket var en garçon (som han udtrykte det), var også der, og selvom han ikke var adjudant, havde han tegnet sig for et stort beløb til udgifterne. Boris var nu en velstående mand, der var steget til høje æresposter og ikke længere søgte protektion, men stod på lige fod med de højeste af sine jævnaldrende. Han mødte Hélène i Vilna, efter ikke at have set hende i lang tid, og mindedes ikke fortiden, men da Hélène nød en meget vigtig personligheds gunst, og Boris kun nylig var blevet gift, mødtes de som gamle venner.

Ved midnat dansede man stadig. Hélène, der ikke havde en passende partner, tilbød selv at danse mazurka med Boris. De var det tredje par. Boris, der køligt betragtede Hélènes blændende, bare skuldre, der stak op af en mørk, guldbroderet gazekjole, talte med hende om gamle bekendte og ophørte samtidig, uden selv at vide det og ubemærket af andre, aldrig et øjeblik med at iagttage kejseren, der befandt sig i det samme rum. Kejseren dansede ikke; han stod i døråbningen og standsede snart det ene par, snart det andet med nådige ord, som kun han forstod at udtale.

Da mazurkaen begyndte, så Boris, at generaladjudant Balasjov, en af dem, der var kejseren nærmest, gik hen til ham og i strid med hofetiketten blev stående nær ham, mens han talte med en polsk dame. Da kejseren var færdig med at tale til hende, kiggede han spørgende på Balasjov, og da han tydeligvis forstod, at han kun handlede sådan, fordi der var vigtige grunde til det, nikkede han let til damen og vendte sig mod ham. Næppe havde Balasjov begyndt at tale, før et udtryk af forbløffelse viste sig på kejserens ansigt. Han tog Balasjov under armen og krydsede salen med ham, mens han ubevidst ryddede en sti på syv alen, da folkene på begge sider veg til side for ham. Boris bemærkede Araktjejevs ophidsede ansigt, da kejseren gik ud med Balasjov. Araktjejev kiggede på kejseren under sine bryn og trådte, snøftende med sin røde næse, et skridt frem fra mængden, som om han ventede, at kejseren ville henvende sig til ham. (Boris forstod, at Araktjejev misundte Balasjov og var utilfreds med, at tydeligvis vigtige nyheder var nået kejseren ad anden vej end gennem ham.)
Men kejseren og Balasjov gik ud i den oplyste have uden at bemærke Araktjejev, der med hånden på kården og et vredt blik omkring sig fulgte tyve skridt bag dem.

Hele den tid Boris dansede mazurkaens figurer, var han optaget af spørgsmålet om, hvilke nyheder Balasjov havde bragt, og hvordan han kunne finde det ud før andre. I den figur, hvor han skulle vælge to damer, hviskede han til Hélène, at han ville vælge grevinde Potocka, som han troede var gået ud på verandaen, og gled hen over parkettet til døren ud til haven, hvor han så Balasjov og kejseren komme tilbage mod verandaen og blev stående. De bevægede sig mod døren. Boris, der flagrede som om han ikke havde nået at trække sig tilbage, pressede sig ærbødigt tæt til dørstolpen med bøjet hoved.
Kejseren, med den ophidselse, der præger en, som er blevet personligt fornærmet, var ved at afslutte med disse ord:

»At gå ind i Rusland uden at erklære krig! Jeg slutter ikke fred, så længe en eneste bevæbnet fjende befinder sig i mit land!« Det forekom Boris, at det glædede kejseren at udtale disse ord. Han var tilfreds med den form, han havde givet sine tanker, men utilfreds med, at Boris havde overhørt det.
»Lad ingen få det at vide!« tilføjede kejseren med rynkede bryn.
Boris forstod, at det var rettet mod ham, og lukkede øjnene og bøjede let hovedet. Kejseren gik ind i balsalen igen og forblev der omkring en halv time mere.

Boris var således den første til at erfare nyheden om, at den franske hær havde krydset Njemen, og takket være dette var han i stand til at vise visse vigtige personligheder, at meget, der var skjult for andre, sædvanligvis var ham bekendt, og herved steg han højere i deres agtelse.

Den uventede nyhed om franskmændenes overskridelse af Njemen var særlig rystende efter en måned med uopfyldte forventninger og ved et bal. Ved den første modtagelse af nyheden, under indtryk af harme og vrede, havde kejseren fundet en vending, der behagede ham, fuldt ud udtrykte hans følelser og siden er blevet berømt. Da han vendte hjem klokken to om natten, sendte han bud efter sin sekretær, Sjisjkov, og bad ham skrive en ordre til tropperne og et reskript til feltmarskal fyrst Saltykov, hvori han insisterede på, at ordene blev indsat, at han ikke ville slutte fred, så længe en eneste bevæbnet franskmand befandt sig på russisk jord.
Næste dag blev følgende brev sendt til Napoleon:
Monsieur mon frère,

I går erfarede jeg, at Deres Majestæts tropper trods den troskab, hvormed jeg har holdt mine forpligtelser over for Deres Majestæt, har krydset den russiske grænse, og jeg har netop modtaget en note fra Petersborg, hvori grev Lauriston som begrundelse for denne aggression meddeler mig, at Deres Majestæt har anset sig for at være i krigstilstand med mig fra det tidspunkt, fyrst Kurakin bad om sine passer. De grunde, hvorpå hertug de Bassano baserede sit afslag på at udlevere dem til ham, ville aldrig have fået mig til at antage, at dette kunne tjene som påskud for aggression. Ambassadøren har faktisk, som han selv har erklæret, aldrig været bemyndiget til at stille det krav, og så snart jeg blev underrettet om det, lod jeg ham vide, hvor meget jeg misbilligede det, og beordrede ham at forblive på sin post. Hvis Deres Majestæt ikke har til hensigt at udgyde vores folks blod for en sådan misforståelse og indvilliger i at trække Deres tropper tilbage fra russisk territorium, vil jeg betragte det skete som ikke sket, og en forståelse mellem os vil være mulig. I modsat fald, Deres Majestæt, vil jeg se mig nødsaget til at afslå et angreb, som intet fra min side har fremprovokeret. Det afhænger stadig af Deres Majestæt at bevare menneskeheden fra endnu en krigs ulykke.
Jeg er osv.,
(underskrevet) Alexander

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Emperor of Russia had spent more than a month in Vilna, reviewing troops and holding maneuvers. Nothing was ready for the war that everyone expected, the war the Emperor had come from Petersburg to prepare. There was no general plan of action. The wavering between the various proposed plans had even grown worse after the Emperor had been a month at headquarters. Each of the three armies had its own commander in chief, but no supreme commander led all the forces, and the Emperor did not take that role himself.

The longer the Emperor stayed in Vilna, the less anyone — tired of waiting — got ready for the war. All the efforts of the people around the sovereign seemed aimed at one thing: making him pass his time pleasantly and forget that war was coming.

In June, after many balls and fetes given by the Polish magnates, the courtiers, and the Emperor himself, one of the Polish aides-de-camp in attendance thought the Emperor's aides-de-camp should give him a dinner and ball. The idea was welcomed eagerly, and the Emperor agreed. The aides-de-camp raised the money by subscription. They invited the lady thought most pleasing to the Emperor to be hostess. Count Bennigsen, who owned land in the Vilna province, offered his country house for the fete, and the thirteenth of June was set for a ball, dinner, regatta, and fireworks at Zakret, Count Bennigsen's country seat.

On the very day Napoleon ordered the crossing of the Niemen, and his vanguard drove off the Cossacks and crossed the Russian frontier, Alexander was spending the evening at the entertainment his aides-de-camp were giving at Bennigsen's country house.

It was a gay, brilliant fete. Connoisseurs of such things said that rarely had so many beautiful women been gathered in one place. Among the Russian ladies who had followed the sovereign from Petersburg to Vilna was Countess Bezukhova, whose ample, so-called Russian beauty eclipsed the refined Polish ladies. The Emperor noticed her and honored her with a dance.

Boris Drubetskoy was there too. He had left his wife in Moscow and was for the time being en garçon (as he put it), and though he was no aide-de-camp, he had put a large sum toward the expenses. Boris was now a rich man who had risen to high honors. He no longer looked for patrons but stood on equal terms with the highest of his own age. He was meeting Helene in Vilna after a long time apart and did not think of the past. But Helene was enjoying the favor of a very important personage, and Boris had only recently married, so they met as good friends of long standing.

Dancing was still going on at midnight. Helene had no suitable partner, so she offered herself to dance the mazurka with Boris. They were the third couple. Boris looked coolly at Helene's dazzling bare shoulders, which rose out of a dark gauze gown embroidered with gold, and talked to her about old acquaintances. All the while, without knowing it himself and without anyone noticing, he never stopped watching the Emperor, who was in the same room. The Emperor was not dancing. He stood in the doorway and stopped couple after couple with the gracious words that only he knew how to say.

Just as the mazurka began, Boris saw Adjutant General Balashev, one of those closest to the Emperor, approach him and, against court etiquette, stand beside him while he was talking to a Polish lady. The Emperor finished speaking to her and gave Balashev a questioning look. He evidently understood that Balashev would act this way only for important reasons, so he gave the lady a slight nod and turned to him. Balashev had barely begun to speak when a look of amazement crossed the Emperor's face. He took Balashev by the arm and walked across the room with him, unconsciously clearing a path seven yards wide as people stepped aside on both sides. Boris noticed Arakcheev's excited face as the sovereign left with Balashev. Arakcheev looked at the Emperor from under his brow and, sniffing through his red nose, stepped out of the crowd as though expecting the Emperor to address him. (Boris understood that Arakcheev envied Balashev and was displeased that evidently important news had reached the Emperor some way other than through himself.)
But the Emperor and Balashev passed out into the lighted garden without noticing Arakcheev, who followed some twenty paces behind, holding his sword and glancing angrily about.

Throughout the figures of the mazurka, Boris was worried by one question: what news had Balashev brought, and how could he learn it before the others? In the figure where he had to choose two ladies, he whispered to Helene that he meant to choose Countess Potocka, who, he thought, had gone out onto the veranda. Then he glided across the parquet to the door that opened onto the garden. There he saw Balashev and the Emperor coming back toward the veranda, and he stopped. They were heading for the door. Boris, fluttering as if he hadn't had time to get out of the way, pressed himself respectfully against the doorpost with his head bowed.
The Emperor, agitated like a man who has been personally insulted, was finishing with these words:

"To enter Russia without declaring war! I will not make peace as long as a single armed enemy remains in my country!" It seemed to Boris that the Emperor took pleasure in saying this. He was pleased with how he had put his thoughts, but displeased that Boris had overheard.
"Let no one know of it!" the Emperor added with a frown.
Boris understood that this was meant for him, and closing his eyes, he bowed his head slightly. The Emperor went back into the ballroom and stayed about another half hour.

So Boris was the first to hear that the French army had crossed the Niemen. This let him show certain important personages that he often knew things hidden from others, and in that way he rose in their esteem.

The unexpected news that the French had crossed the Niemen was especially startling after a month of expectations that came to nothing, and at a ball. When the news first reached him, the Emperor, in his indignation and resentment, had hit on a phrase that pleased him, expressed his feelings fully, and has since become famous. He got home at two o'clock that night and sent for his secretary, Shishkov. He told him to write an order to the troops and a rescript to Field Marshal Prince Saltykov, and insisted that the words be put in that he would not make peace as long as a single armed Frenchman remained on Russian soil.
The next day this letter went to Napoleon:
Monsieur mon frère,

Yesterday I learned that your troops have crossed the Russian frontier, in spite of the loyalty with which I have kept my engagements to Your Majesty. This very moment I have received from Petersburg a note in which Count Lauriston gives me the reason for this aggression: Your Majesty has considered yourself at war with me ever since Prince Kurakin asked for his passports. The reasons the Duc de Bassano gave for refusing them to him would never have led me to suppose that this could serve as a pretext for aggression. In fact the ambassador, as he himself has declared, was never authorized to make that demand, and as soon as I was informed of it I told him how much I disapproved and ordered him to remain at his post. If Your Majesty does not intend to shed the blood of our peoples over such a misunderstanding, and agrees to withdraw your troops from Russian territory, I will treat what has passed as though it had not occurred, and an understanding between us will be possible. Otherwise, Your Majesty, I shall find myself forced to repel an attack that nothing on my part has provoked. It still depends on Your Majesty to spare humanity the calamity of another war.
I am, etc.,
(signed) Alexander
